extracted.intended_audience: literate newspaper readers and essayists (early 18th-century); writers of moral/persuasive essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing agreeable, persuasive writing—especially advice, fables, and moral or poetic pieces—that pleases readers and instructs without giving offence. Emphasises techniques to render counsel palatable and engage reader participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of making advice agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing so difficult as the Art of making Advice agreeable; we look upon the Man who gives it us as offering an Affront to our Understanding, and treating us like Children or Ideots. Writers are distinguished according to the Perfection at which they have arrived in this Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explicit, blunt instruction that reads as censure. Recognise that advice implies a superiority and will be resented unless delivered skilfully. The author notes that writers vary in how well they disguise instruction: by diction, verse, wit, or proverb. Example: the popularity of Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel rests not only on poetry but on a plan that engages the reader in discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use oblique/indirect methods (fables) to give counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: The oblique manner of giving Advice is so inoffensive, that if we look into ancient Histories, we find the wise Men of old very often chose to give Counsel to their Kings in Fables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer indirect presentation—fables, allegories, or stories—when advising, especially about sensitive matters. The essay gives the Turkish tale of Sultan Mahmoud as an example of a fable that moved a ruler to reform. Indirection prevents the recipient feeling affronted and increases receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reader a participant (enable discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mind is never so much pleased, as when she exerts her self in any Action that gives her an Idea of her own Perfections and Abilities. In Writings of this kind, the Reader comes in for half of the Performance; every thing appears to him like a Discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure work so readers can apply characters and circumstances themselves and 'discover' meanings—this active involvement heightens pleasure and persuasiveness. Example: the popularity of Absalom and Achitophel is attributed to the plan that allows the reader to 'exert his own Talents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Devices to render exhortation palatable (diction, versification, wit, proverbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many Devices have been made use of, to render this bitter Potion palatable? Some convey their Instructions to us in the best chosen Words, others in the most harmonious Numbers, some in Points of Wit, and others in short Proverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offering instruction, choose among techniques to soften the delivery: precise/chosen wording; harmonious verse or cadence; humour/wit to disarm; concise proverbs to encapsulate the lesson. Use examples and stylistic variation appropriate to the audience and subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of effective poetic style for calming reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgil is praised as writing 'so divine, so harmonious, nor so equal a Strain, which leaves the Mind composed, and softened into an agreeable Melancholy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works intended to soothe or close the day (meditative/reflective pieces), aim for harmony, balance, and a measured, even strain that composes the reader. The example recommends choosing authors/tones that produce agreeable melancholy and composure (Virgil as model).
